dialogs.title: Dialogue — Nima boʻldi?
dialogs.intro: Budi has missed class for two days. Nilufar comes to the dorm with a bag of fruit.

notes: **Boshim ogʻriyapti — it's your head that hurts, not you.** Uzbek places pain **in the body part**, and that body part is the subject of the sentence. Literally "my head is hurting". English does something similar with "my head hurts", but Uzbek uses this pattern for every ache — never "I have a headache".

**Kasal boʻldim = "I fell ill".** *Boʻlmoq* marks a **change** of state: *kasal boʻldim* (became sick), *charchadim* (got tired), *katta boʻldi* (grew up). Whereas *kasalman* means "I'm sick" without saying when it started.
**Ikki kundan beri = "for two days now".** *-dan beri* means "since", and it pairs with the ongoing form: *Ikki kundan beri yomgʻir yogʻyapti* (it's been raining for two days).

**Sizsiz = "without you".** The *-siz* ending from unit 13 attached to a pronoun. Note that it looks just like the predicate ending *-siz* (you are) — only its position and meaning in the sentence tell them apart.

grammars.title: Complaining of pain: three patterns
body: All three are used interchangeably in everyday conversation. The first is the most common.
after: ⚠️ Body parts **must take a possessive ending**. *Bosh ogʻriyapti* sounds like "some head is hurting" with no owner — odd. Always *boshim*, *boshingiz*, *boshi*.
Remember the vowel-dropping from unit 3, which happens a lot with body parts: *ogʻiz* → *ogʻzim*, *burun* → *burnim*, *qorin* → *qornim*, *koʻngil* → *koʻnglim*.
Use the past to talk about pain that's over: *Kecha boshim ogʻridi* (my head hurt yesterday). Use the habitual for chronic pain: *Qishda tizzam ogʻriydi* (my knee hurts in winter).

grammars.title: Boʻlmoq: the verb that changes states
body: One verb, many jobs. It covers "become", "happen", "may", and "OK" in the sense of agreeing.
after: *Boʻladi* on its own is one of the most frequently heard words in Uzbekistan. It means "OK", "sure", "done" — an all-purpose answer that's always safe.
*Boʻlsin* means "may it be": *Salomat boʻling!* (stay healthy), *Omadingiz boʻlsin!* (good luck), *Osh boʻlsin!* (enjoy your meal).
⚠️ Don't mix up *boʻlmoq* with *bor*. *Bor* says something **already exists**; *boʻlmoq* says something **comes into being** or **changes**.

blocks.text: Say each word while pointing to the part, then repeat with the ending *-im*. Two rounds and this list will stick.

⚠️ *Yurak* means the **heart** both as an organ and as the seat of feelings — just like English "heart". *Jigar* is the liver, and it's also used as a term of endearment for a child: *jigarim* = "my darling".

*Koʻngil* is a word worth knowing even though it isn't a body part: it means "heart, soul, feelings". *Koʻnglim toʻq* (I'm at peace), *koʻngil ochmoq* (to have fun), *koʻnglingizga olmang* (don't take it personally).

sections.title: At the pharmacy and the doctor's

blocks.text: Pharmacies in Uzbekistan sell many medicines without a prescription, and pharmacists readily give advice — often it's the first stop before seeing a doctor.

blocks.text: *Tez yordam* literally means "quick help" and is the word for ambulance; the number is 103. Other emergency numbers: police 102, fire 101, gas 104.
